newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel sees light side of German tax row.
newsitem.headline: Waigel sees light side of German tax row.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel, the German politician with the least to laugh about these days, has found a way to make light of the budget woes besetting Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government.

Taking a break from the wrangling over tax and pension reform in Bonn, Waigel donned a medieval coat of mail and a jester's cap at the weekend to accept the annual Order Against Deadly Seriousness from a carnival club in Aachen.

"Everybody can laugh about something funny, but the real humour begins when the taxman comes and the finance minister gets an award for sending him!" he quipped in his acceptance speech broadcast on television late on Sunday evening.
"How can Waigel help you make a small fortune?" he asked the hall packed with prominent politicians and celebrities. "First, you start with a large fortune..."
The humour and the costume were par for the course for Carnival, the Mardi Gras-style "fifth season" when Rhinelanders party, parade and parody anyone in power.

Waigel, Bonn's chief tax collector since 1989, stands at the centre of a mounting row over tax and pension reform that could cloud Kohl's re-election chances in 1998 if he does not work some supply-side magic and create more jobs.

One up-and-coming young leader in Kohl's Christian Democratic (CDU) party, Lower Saxony state CDU chief Christian Wulff, has already written off the planned reform as too little, too late and called on the finance minister to quit.
Waigel fired back with a pun, saying he would turn "even a cowardly sheep in Wulff's clothing into mutton goulash".

As for other critics within Kohl's centre-right coalition, Waigel observed wryly that "when I'm under fire, my loyal friends courageously stand up to shield me -- as long as they know I'm only being shot in the back.
"When the spears come from the front, they're 100 percent behind me," he said at the ceremony on Saturday evening.

In keeping with the Carnival spirit, Waigel aimed his barbs at himself as well, inventing a story about how three boys saved him from drowning after the ice cracked on a frozen lake he was walking across.
Waigel said he offered the boys any present they would like for saving his life. The first wanted a toy train set and the second a bicycle -- no problem there.
The third stunned him by asking for a state funeral. When Waigel asked him why, the boy answered: "When I go home and say I pulled you out of the water, my father will kill me!"
